coherence.reasons: X's governing thought (enter via Amazon, reject retail, hold Japan) is carried by five summary claims that each map to a slide, and the decisions requested follow from the sensitivities shown. Its envelope ($5M), triggers (28% ACoS) and re-basing (30–32%) are consistent with its own scenario table, and it states that the 38% case would exceed the envelope. Y is also logically ordered around five sub-questions, but it has internal tensions. It calls $3.9M the 'worst-case peak cash need' and says 'the cap holds in every case we ran', while its own stall case reaches -$6.8M and its 38% ACoS case -$6.4M. Its backup says to 'use 32%' ACoS, at which payback fails, while the governing thought promises payback through a 28.6% ceiling set exactly at break-even with no buffer. Its section on the US versus Japan argues mostly from revenue, not from the board's tests.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation (Amazon-led with gates, retail only above 20% awareness, $40M not reachable by 2030). X weighs the alternatives more fully. It compares Japan on cash as well as revenue and concedes that J beats A at 32% ACoS (+$1.8M vs -$2.3M), then argues strategic value and brings Japan back as a 2028 case. It sizes a $5M board envelope against a combined downside, adds a door-test gate and an affordability gate for retail, and tells the board plainly that at the benchmark ACoS payback slips past 2030. Y adds a useful stall case with an end-2027 stop rule (loss capped near $2.5M) and an explicit restatement of the ambition. But it treats Japan mostly on revenue, sets the ACoS gate at the break-even itself, and does not address how capping ad spend affects volume. X at least shows volume sensitivities at 80% and 70% of plan.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key's numbers: $4.73 and $7.55 unit contributions, B peak $20.8M, group margin 4.5%, A at +2.4 / +0.4 / -2.3 across ACoS cases, 28.6% break-even, 26.9% with tariff. Both reject the $5.2B figure, the 4.5 units per door and the halo correlation. X adds corrected-B cases ($26.4M cash need, $28.3M revenue), volume and combined sensitivities, the CEO's 2029 retail add-on, the slowdown in pilot growth from 17% to 9% a month, and flags its own judgement calls. Y's stall calculation is correct and it shows the break-even arithmetic. But it over-reads Saebom ('added doors only after reaching about $30M on Amazon', where the pack gives $30M total US revenue in the same year the doors were added) and leans on Saebom for the '$40M after retail' path. It labels $3.9M as worst case despite worse cases of its own, and its 'Mooncrest pattern would repeat' rests on a single case. Y also shows minor rounding inconsistencies (9.45% vs 9.4%).

revision.reasons: Both keep the CEO's Amazon-first hypothesis with conditions, which is what the key expects. Both raise the retail trigger from 15% to 20% using Table 8, replace the 25% ACoS assumption, and reset the $40M ambition. Y has an explicit from-to slide on the hypothesis and formally asks the board to restate $40M as a goal beyond 2030. X goes one step further on the hypothesis's second half: it models 'CEO plan + B-scale retail in 2029' (-$11.8M cash, 6.3% margin) to show why retail needs an affordability gate and a door test, and it re-bases the plan at 30–32% ACoS. Both are strong; X tests the hypothesis slightly more rigorously.

overall.reasons: Both documents are sound and land on the defensible recommendation with correct core calculations. X would serve the board better. It scores every option on all five board tests, is candid that payback probably slips at benchmark ad costs, and compares Japan honestly on cash. It quantifies a wider set of downside cases and turns them into a concrete cash envelope, triggers with responses, and four retail gates. Y's stall case with a stop rule and its from-to framing are valuable, but its 'worst-case' labelling contradicts its own cases, its ACoS ceiling has no buffer, and its Japan trade-off is thin.
